summary: The note surveys how seasonal rituals and their folktales are being revived and reshaped by modern culture and technology, using four 2023-2024 events tied to the equinoxes and solstices. Each event blends traditional myths with podcasts, live streams, VR, and eco-friendly practices. It concludes that while delivery has shifted from oral to digital, storytelling still connects past, present, and future.
one_line: Four 2023-2024 seasonal festivals show ancient equinox and solstice folktales being reinvented through digital media, VR, and environmental themes.
key_facts: Alice Greenwood, a folklorist, organized an outdoor Autumnal Equinox festival on September 23, 2023, in Vermont.
At the Vermont festival, storytellers gathered around bonfires, and tales of corn spirits and harvest deities were amplified through podcasts and live streams.
The autumn event highlighted agritourism, social media for sharing regional folklore, and seasonal foods central to Thanksgiving myths.
Influencer Julian Torres, with millions of followers, began a campaign on December 22, 2023, to globally stream Winter Solstice celebrations and folk performances.
Torres's campaign featured interactive VR experiences of sun-rebirth myths, and the tales of the Holly King and the Oak King circulated online.
Evelyn Carpenter, a community organizer in Savannah, Georgia, infused the March 20, 2024 Spring Equinox festivals with traditional and unconventional folklore.
Carpenter's Spring Festival drew on the Easter Bunny and the goddess Persephone, using theatrical performances, music, dance, and virtual reality installations.
The spring festival offered lessons on sustainability and nature's cycles, relevant to environmental concerns.
The summer solstice on June 21, 2024, was celebrated in Stonehaven, Scotland, where Zara MacTavish initiated the 'Blazing Bonfire Project' to rekindle interest in age-old fire customs.
In Stonehaven, modern druids and pagans blended ancient Celtic traditions with theatrical pyrotechnics, music festivals, and eco-friendly firework alternatives.
The summer stories became rallying points for addressing climate change and renewable energy.
The note says oral storytelling now shares space with podcasts, social media, virtual gatherings, and augmented reality as the new gathering places for myth-telling.
